12847-havelok-the-dane-a-legend-of-old-g:
Charles W. Whistler retold the ancient legend of Havelok the Dane as a tale of old Grimsby and Lincoln. Grim the fisher and his sons shelter the boy Havelok, son of Gunnar, who crosses the swan's path, survives storm and shipwreck, and helps found Grimsby town. Years as cook's boy and porter, under the name Curan, hide his royal birth.

In Lincoln marketplace Havelok, strong and hungry, takes loaves from Berthun and shares them, while crowds watch the big stranger with respect and wariness. A strange wedding and a Danish jarl follow. Whistler's retelling keeps the old story's wonder for modern young readers.
1815-the-boys-life-of-abraham-lincoln:
Helen Nicolay writes Lincoln's life for boys, opening with his forefathers, pioneers who left their homes to open the wilderness and make the way plain for others. For a hundred and seventy years, she notes, the family had moved west ahead of settlement, and Lincoln's own childhood followed that pattern.

The book follows him from log cabin to law office to White House. It does not flinch from the hard parts: the shadow of the Capitol dome, the question of slavery in the states, and the war that tested him. Written by the daughter of Lincoln's secretary, it carries a family closeness to its subject, and it remains a clear first biography for young readers.
18379-abraham-lincoln:
Lord Charnwood wrote this life of Abraham Lincoln, published in Garden City, New York, in 1917, with copyright by Henry Holt. Charnwood's general editor opens by noting that statesmen rarely win the unquestioning recognition given to warriors, scientists, artists, and poets, since a statesman's work lacks a single decisive measure. Lincoln, the book argues, earns that recognition over time, as evidence accumulates.

Chapters follow Lincoln's boyhood, the growth of the American nation, his early career at New Salem and in the Illinois legislature, his marriage, his time in Congress and retirement, and his rise. The subject, Charnwood says, is revered as preserver of the commonwealth, with an affection seldom given to statesmen, shared even by those whose fathers fought against him. Readers get a classic short life: Lincoln the lawyer, politician, and war president, judged with cool English fairness.
18540-abraham-lincoln:
Rev. T. M. Eddy gave this memorial discourse at a union meeting in the Presbyterian church at Waukegan, Illinois, on Wednesday, April 19, 1865, the day of Lincoln's funeral services in Washington. The meeting was held as an act of public mourning, and citizens who heard the address asked Eddy to publish it.

The discourse praises Lincoln's life and death, and frames his work as service to a loyal nation in wartime. It stands as a record of how one Midwestern town grieved the murdered president in the week after his death, and how a local minister put that grief into words for print.
22925-the-story-of-young-abraham-lincoln:
Wayne Whipple tells The Story of Young Abraham Lincoln for young readers. With all his brain and brawn, Whipple writes, Lincoln's real greatness lay in his heart. Whipple calls him the great-hearted man of the White House. Far more people know Lincoln's name, he adds, than ever met Bunyan's Great-Heart on the page.

The biography follows Lincoln from log-cabin childhood toward the presidency, stressing kindness, honesty, and hard study. Whipple shapes true events into episodes a child can hold, the rail fence, the borrowed book, the wrestling match. Such lives of Lincoln filled schoolrooms for decades. This one keeps the period's reverent tone, and its Bunyan comparison shows how Americans framed their hero.
6811-the-life-of-abraham-lincoln:
Henry Ketcham dedicates his Life of Abraham Lincoln to his two older brothers, who served under Lincoln as commander-in-chief in the war for union and the end of slavery. Chapters run from the wild west and the Lincoln family through early years in Indiana, a second journey to New Orleans, desultory jobs, and entry into politics and law. Social life, marriage, and the slave power's encroachments follow.

The awakening of the lion, the birth of the Republican Party, and the battle of the giants lead toward the presidency. Ketcham writes for young readers, with admiration and clarity. The Life of Abraham Lincoln is a warm, readable introduction to a great American life.
7547-quotes-and-images-from-the-writings:
Abraham Lincoln's writings fill eight volumes. They run from his first political address in 1832 to a hastily scrawled note on the day of his assassination. This volume gathers quotations from them with images. The editor hoped that quotations scrolling beside steel engravings and photographs of Lincoln might give the words greater impact. The design of the original page aimed at exactly that.

The entries trace the arc of Lincoln's public life. They touch the abolition of slavery in Washington, and the hundred thousand slaves then in United States military service. They show his resolve to act in such a manner as to create no bad feeling. The collection lets a reader browse Lincoln's mind in fragments, from young politician to president, and then follow any quotation to its full context.
906-abraham-lincoln:
James Russell Lowell writes an essay on Abraham Lincoln, the president he watched through the Civil War, praising his humour, patience, and growth in office. Lowell, a poet and critic, saw Lincoln as a truly American statesman. Lowell wrote the essay during the Civil War, when Lincoln's leadership was still doubted.

The essay weighs Lincoln's speeches, his handling of generals and parties, and his moral steadiness under war. It remains a classic contemporary judgment, written by a man who knew the stakes and admired the man. His praise for Lincoln's humour and patience has lasted, since later writers echoed it.
abraham-lincoln:
James Russell Lowell writes on Abraham Lincoln while the Civil War still rages and Lincoln still sits in the White House. Lowell, a poet and critic, sizes up a president many in the East had dismissed as a rough westerner. The essay argues that Lincoln's plain sense, patience, and honesty fit the crisis exactly.

He weighs Lincoln's speeches and acts, his handling of generals and factions, and his slow movement on slavery. Lowell's prose is careful and warm, rising at the close to real eloquence. Coming from a leading man of letters, the piece helped fix Lincoln's standing with educated readers who had doubted him.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-abbey-of-eins:
The Catholic Encyclopedia entry on Einsiedeln describes a Benedictine monastery in Schwyz, Switzerland, named for Our Lady of the Hermits. The place takes its name from its hermit founders. St. Meinrad, educated at Reichenau, embraced the hermit's life on Mount Etzel with a wonder-working statue of Our Lady given by Abbess Hildegard of Zurich.

Robbers murdered Meinrad in 861 for the shrine's treasures, yet hermits kept his place for eighty years. Then Eberhard, former provost of Strasburg, built a monastery and church and became its first abbot. Legend says the church gained a miraculous consecration, and pilgrims have crowded Einsiedeln ever since. The entry follows the shrine from hermitage to great abbey.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-blessed-chris:
Blessed Christine of Stommeln, a mystic, is the subject of this 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia entry. Born at Stommeln near Cologne in 1242 to a well-to-do peasant, Heinrich Bruso, she died in 1312. At five she saw visions of the Christ Child, her mystic spouse from age ten, and at eleven she learned to read the Psalter, though she could not write.

When her parents sought a marriage for her at twelve, she fled to the Beguines at Cologne, a community of devout women, and lived a life of severe penance. Visions, stigmata, and demonic torments fill her later story, recorded by her Dominican confessor. The entry presents a peasant girl of extraordinary inner life.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-saint-hugh-of:
Hugh of Lincoln, born about 1135 at Avalon in Burgundy and dead at London on 16 November 1200, was the son of William, Lord of Avalon, and his wife Anna. After Anna's death William retired to the Augustinian monastery of Villard-Benoît near Grenoble, taking Hugh with him, and Hugh became a religious and was ordained deacon at nineteen. About 1159 he was sent as prior to the priory of Saint-Maximin near his old home.

Longing for a fully contemplative life, he visited the Grande Chartreuse with the prior of Villard-Benoît. He sought to join the Carthusians, though his superior first made him vow to give up the idea. Judging that vow, made without due thought, not binding, he returned as a novice in 1153 and later became procurator of the Chartreuse. In 1180 he left to become prior of Witham in Somerset, England's first Carthusian house.
quotes-and-images-from-the-writings-of-a:
Quotes and Images from Abraham Lincoln, prepared by David Widger, gathers quotations and subject references from the eight volumes of The Writings of Abraham Lincoln. Widger's note sets the span. It runs from Lincoln's first political address in 1832. It ends with a hastily scrawled note on the day of his assassination. Steel engravings and photographs are included. They are meant to give the words greater impact.

The extracts open in war: a hundred thousand former slaves now serve in the United States military, slavery is abolished in Washington, and "the war came." Lincoln's rule stands here in his own words: as he would not be a slave, so he would not be a master.
the-boys-life-of-abraham-lincoln:
Helen Nicolay wrote The Boys' Life of Abraham Lincoln. The first part, A President's Childhood, traces his stock. His forefathers were pioneers who left home to open the wilds for those who came after. The first of them reached Massachusetts from England in 1638. For one hundred and seventy years since, the line had moved slow west.

Kentucky was his birthplace, on February 12, 1809. There his parents lived in deep want, in a rude log cabin. Nicolay calls Lincoln a pioneer of a nobler sort, one who led men's thoughts toward the right. His tale starts and ends in blood. His grandfather Abraham was shot by an Indian while at work with his three sons on their clearing. Mordecai, the eldest, shot the Indian who stooped to seize small Thomas, age six, and held the cabin till help came from the fort.
the-life-of-abraham-lincoln: Henry Ketcham wrote his life of Abraham Lincoln and dedicated it to two older brothers who served under Lincoln in the Civil War. Only the title page, dedication, and contents are present here. Chapters run from the wild West and the Lincoln family through Indiana years. Law practice, slavery debates, the nomination of 1860, Fort Sumter, and emancipation follow in the list. The biography itself does not appear here beyond those chapter titles.
the-southerner-a-romance-of-the-real-lin: Thomas Dixon subtitled this novel a romance of the real Lincoln, publishing it with D. Appleton and Company in New York and London in 1913, with illustrations by J. N. Marchand. The pages present here are front matter only. A Walt Whitman remark calls Lincoln essentially a Southern contribution. A dedication honours Woodrow Wilson as the first Southern-born president since Lincoln and Dixon's friend and collegemate. A list of Dixon's other novels includes The Leopard's Spots and The Clansman, so the story itself does not appear.
